author: Forbes
description:
How does a scrappy $900 parking lot pop-up with a Home Depot fryer transform into a $1 billion valuation in just a few years? On this episode of Built Different, Dave's Hot Chicken CEO Jim Bitticks breaks down the radically unconventional playbook behind the brand's explosive growth to 500 locations. Jim reveals why the company actively ignores industry consultants who push for faster drive-thru times, why corporate executives are encouraged to buy their own franchises, and how an unprecedented private equity buyout was structured to share the wealth and mint 19 employee millionaires.

author: Forbes
description:
In early 2021, Anthropic cofounder Dario Amodei was looking for investors for his nascent AI model startup. One of the people he approached was Jaan Tallinn, an Estonian programmer and investor who was one of the cofounders of video calling platform Skype.

Not long after Tallinn and his cofounders sold the company to eBay for $2.6 billion in 2005, Tallinn became deeply interested in—and worried about—artificial intelligence. By 2008, long before he sat down with Amodei, he had become convinced that AI could threaten humanity’s survival. That belief crystallized during a meeting with Eliezer Yudkowsky, a well-known AI safety researcher and cofounder of the nonprofit Machine Intelligence Research Institute, at a Panera Bread near Millbrae, California in 2009.

Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as the company’s CEO on Monday, saying its decision was based on quote “input from senior levels of the United States government.” This shocking reversal came after the board had earlier ousted Huang over allegations of multiple extramarital affairs, including with a suspected Chinese spy.

Nvidia’s board released a statement Monday saying it had reinstalled Huang quote “effective immediately.” The CEO previously resigned November 12th amid reports of him having affairs with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese asset, and with Nvidia executive Kimberly Powell.

author: Forbes
description:
Five-time Grammy winner Angélique Kidjo was just a teenager when the radio started playing only propaganda music in Benin, a country in West Africa where a coup instated a communist dictatorship.

The music icon sat down with Senior Editor Alex Knapp to discuss how she moved to Paris to study music, which she describes as something out of a spy novel, and eventually found her way to the United States, where she uses music to tell the stories of her ancestors.
